How we evaluated these platforms The 11 best returns management solutions of 2026 Buyer’s checklist: six questions to ask every vendor How to choose your vendor for managing returns and improving the customer experience Gain access to our choosing the right returns management solution guide. Download now Returns management solutions don’t just decide how much revenue you keep from sales. According to Katherine Cullen at the National Retail Federation , they’re “an additional touchpoint for retailers to provide a positive interaction with their customers.” The scale is huge. The National Retail Federation estimated that retailers would receive $849.9 billion in returns in 2025 , equal to 15.8% of annual sales. And customers remember a poor process. In the same research, 71% said they would be less likely to shop with a retailer again after a bad returns experience. The right returns management software helps you convert returns into revenue without disrupting customer loyalty. You can apply different rules by product or market, then offer an exchange or store credit when it makes sense. Fraud controls flag suspicious requests. Collecting data on return reasons helps you spot recurring product issues, like when one clothing size keeps coming back far more often than others. This guide compares 11 options based on product depth and business needs, helping you narrow the list to what fits you best. What is returns management software? Returns management software handles a return from start to finish. Customers submit requests through a self-service portal, where the platform checks whether each item meets your return policy. If approved, it provides return instructions and tracks the item on its journey. More advanced platforms can also issue refunds, arrange exchanges and update your inventory, streamlining reverse logistics. For example, your warehouse can send an undamaged item straight back into stock. What returns management solutions handle Returns software connects the customer experience with your warehouse and support teams. The main benefit is reducing manual work during reverse logistics while maintaining customer satisfaction. It can: Let customers request a return through a branded self-service return portal . Check each request against the return window and policy for that order. Create a return record (RMA) with a shipping label or QR code. Issue a refund or replacement. Some platforms can also offer exchanges and store credit, which helps you retain revenue. Track the parcel and send updates so customers don’t have to contact support about delayed refunds or package arrivals. Inform the warehouse how to handle each item, then update the order and inventory management records. Show actionable insights on which products come back most often and why. Every step uses the same return record. This means your team spends less time copying information between systems or correcting mistakes. Customers get clearer choices and faster updates. You see where delays and avoidable costs block you from full operational efficiency. Who needs returns management software? Consider dedicated software for returns management processes if: Your support team consistently wastes time on copying return and order details between systems. Too many returns end in refunds. You rarely offer an exchange or store credit instead. Customers contact you because they can’t see their return status or expected refund date. International returns cost too much because parcels take inefficient routes. Your in-store and online return rules don’t match. You suspect return abuse but lack enough data to decide which requests need review. If you run a very small ecommerce business, a clear policy and an organized support queue may be enough. Track returns during a normal month and your busiest sales period. Then calculate how much staff time they take. Dedicated software makes sense once that manual work piles up and costs real money over time. How we evaluated these platforms We evaluated each vendor using the same five areas covered in the profiles below: Primary use case. We identified the type of retailer each platform suits and the returns problem it helps the team handle. Customer return experience. We reviewed how customers start a return and which return methods they can use. We also checked the available refund alternatives, including exchanges or store credit. Policy and risk controls. We examined eligibility rules and return fees. We also reviewed controls for suspicious requests or repeated return abuse. Returns operations. We looked at return labels and status updates. We also considered warehouse processing or international routing where relevant. Integrations and reporting appear when they affect the platform’s main use case. Customer feedback. We recorded the G2 rating available for each vendor in September 2026. We then used recent reviews to identify practical limitations. Your CX and ops teams can give customers a branded self-service return portal and apply the right policy to each request. Set return windows or fees based on customer risk, or offer an exchange or store credit before issuing a refund. Your team can handle warranty claims and gift returns within the same returns management process. Warehouse staff can scan returned items when they arrive and pass return merchandise authorization (RMA) data to your WMS. Send branded updates, compare return rates by SKU or market and identify recurring reasons. Your technical team can connect the returns management software to existing systems through an API or webhook. Key capabilities: Branded self-service return portal: Give customers a portal that matches your brand. You can host it on a separate page, embed it in your site, or use a headless setup. Policy and fraud controls: Set eligibility by product or return reason. Change the return window or fee based on customer risk and route suspicious return requests for review. Flexible return resolutions: Offer exchanges or store credit before cash refunds. Add bonus credit or let an eligible customer keep an item for a partial refund. Complex returns: Handle warranty claims with photo uploads. Accept gift returns or requests without an order number. Split a return when items need different processing routes. Reverse logistics and warehouse processing: Give eligible customers a printable return label or QR code. Use the Return Processing App to scan returned items at a warehouse or store. blogs.author: Jax Connelly
blogs.content: How UGC Builds Trust and Loyalty Generated by Klaviyo AI User-generated content gives shoppers authentic evidence from real customers, helping build purchase confidence, trust, and brand advocacy. The article explains four main UGC types, their business benefits, and practical ways to collect and use customer content and feedback. Four UGC types: Visual content, social posts, reviews and testimonials, and Q&As help customers understand products and brands. Authentic social proof: Real customer experiences can bridge the online shopping gap and make purchase decisions feel more credible. Community and advocacy: UGC encourages two-way communication and can turn customers into loyal brand advocates. Efficient content creation: Organic or paid customer content can be repurposed across marketing channels while reducing production demands. Sign up Get a demo Show AI generated summary In January 2019, when the company was much smaller, italist received “one of the best unprompted endorsements” from an influencer on Instagram, recalls CEO Diego Abba. Dorothy Wang, daughter of billionaire Roger Wang and star of reality show Rich Kids of Beverly Hills , shared this photo with her 1 million followers, crediting italist with helping her find the Louboutin So Kate pumps that completed her birthday outfit: Dorothy Wang’s Instagram “Those who follow my stories might remember that I couldn’t find these Louboutin So Kates in my size to complete my birthday ensemble anywhere,” Wang wrote in her caption. “I am so happy my savvy friend KC Sukamto told me about italist and I want to share it with anyone searching for a hard-to-find item!” “My shoes also ended up being a little less than what I would normally pay (yay for Italian pricing) and the automatic express two-day shipping got them to me in time for the festivities,” she added. “Happy birthday to me!” The thank-you note was spontaneous and completely organic, Abba says: Wang had no prior engagement with italist, but “she highlighted very well the two key advantages of our site: the vast selection from luxury brands, and the lower pricing.” Wang’s post received nearly 35,000 likes—and it’s a perfect example of the power of user-generated content (UGC). More than any other kind of marketing, UGC allows you to talk with your customers, rather than at them. It’s “a key part of the two-way communication that we have with our consumers, thanks to technology and social media,” Abba says. That makes UGC a perfect fit for a brand like italist, whose online store gives shoppers access to when-in-Rome pricing ( up to 40% lower than the rest of the world) and 350,000+ SKUs from independent Italian boutiques, from anywhere with an internet connection. “Not many brands or retailers in the luxury space actively use UGC, in part because the luxury business is built on exclusivity, not inclusion,” Abba points out. “We see our work as democratizing luxury in a small way, making pricey things a bit less pricey, and providing another option for shoppers beyond traditional department stores or having to buy directly from a brand.” In the same way italist is democratizing luxury fashion, then, UGC democratizes content production by flattening traditional top-down media and advertising hierarchies. “UGC makes sense to recognize and reward new customers, loyal customers, and build a strong community around our business,” Abba explains. Not all UGC comes from influencers with large social followings. But all of it can be instrumental in turning one-time shoppers into lifelong brand advocates. Read on to learn how. What is UGC? UGC is original content customers share that brands can use in their marketing efforts. Essentially, it’s today’s version of word-of-mouth marketing: anything people are saying or showing about your brand, online, to their own followers and networks. And it’s crucial: according to the 2026 Bazaarvoice Shopper Experience Index (Volume 18) , two-thirds of Americans and Canadians rely on UGC to make buying decisions. Typically, UGC showcases how real people are using your product in their daily lives. Some UGC, however, might fall more into the realm of lifestyle content, stuff that showcases how your customers’ values align with your brand’s ethos. Since italist, for example, sells 2,500 brands but not products under their own name, UGC that falls into the latter category is particularly valuable: “stories about italist as a useful service and a seamless experience,” Abba says, “rather than simply posts which include an item purchased from italist.” Most UGC is organic, like Wang’s italist shout-out above. But brands can also pay creators to make it. Both types of UGC have their benefits: the former is more raw and unadulterated, while the latter gives the brand more control over content scripts and visuals. But either way, with UGC, your audience takes an active, participatory role in your marketing. Here’s an even easier way to think about it: If the content is associated with your brand but wasn’t officially created by your brand, it’s probably UGC. The 4 main types of UGC UGC comes in many forms. “It’s more than just text,” explains Shaun Lin, former director of channel partnerships at Bazaarvoice , a UGC software platform that enables brands and retailers to collect and display several types of UGC on a variety of channels. “It’s images, it’s video, it’s everything.” “There’s no one size fits all,” agrees Ben Schreiber, CMO at Latico Leathers and co-founder of Forbes-rated boutique ecommerce agency Brand Caffeine , which specializes in paid ads, email and text marketing, SEO, and UGC content creation. “It’s really different for every product and every brand.” The 4 main types of UGC include: 1. Visual UGC Visual UGC refers to photos and videos shared by customers who are interacting with your brand or products. “People want to see real-life photos in addition to the branded photos that companies put on product description pages, and they want to see videos of the product experience: a real person talking about that experience in a real environment, as opposed to a studio-produced video,” Lin explains. Take a look at how pet apparel brand Wild One uses visual UGC to their advantage on their Instagram account . Their posts are a mixture of branded photography and UGC: Wild One’s Instagram Visuals, here, go much further than words would. By displaying a wide variety of pets in various iterations of their products on their feed, Wild One allows potential customers to scroll through for a quick sense of how a Wild One harness might look on their dog, or whether their toys are the right size for their pet. 2. Social media posts Social UGC refers to Instagram stories and posts, TikTok and YouTube videos, and Facebook posts that involve your brand. Because it was 100% organic, Wang’s italist shout-out would qualify as social (and visual) UGC, as would this post from an everyday Instagram user and italist customer: Italist’s tagged Instagram feed 3. Reviews + testimonials Reviews and testimonials refer to any kind of content that involves your customers sharing their opinions and experiences with your brand and products. And they’re particularly crucial for ecommerce brands that do most of their business virtually. According to Klaviyo’s 2025 Future of Consumer Marketing Report , reviews are the No. 1 factor consumers take into account when making a first purchase. Check out these examples from the website homepage of nutrition supplement brand Promix . Notice how customer reviews don’t just have to pertain to your product. They can also speak to less tangible things, like brand values and customer goals. Promix homepage 4. Q&As Q&As allow shoppers to ask questions about products or brands and receive answers from both other customers as well as the brands themselves. This type of UGC not only gives shoppers access to answers they need from sources they trust, but also builds community by inspiring brand experts and pas...

blogs.author: Tiff Regaudie
blogs.content: 2026 Abandoned Cart Flow Benchmarks Generated by Klaviyo AI Analysis of more than 110,000 Klaviyo customers shows that abandoned cart flows generate the highest average revenue per recipient across email and text messaging. The benchmarks also highlight engagement differences among welcome, browse abandonment, and cart abandonment flows, plus ways to test and optimize performance. Highest revenue: Abandoned cart flows average $6.77 in revenue per recipient for email and $4.48 for text messaging. Top performers: The top 10% of brands reach $13.70 in email revenue per recipient and $8.69 for text messaging. Strong engagement: Average abandoned cart click rates are 6% for email and 10.3% for text messaging. Flow diversity: Welcome and browse abandonment flows can match or exceed abandoned cart engagement depending on the channel and industry. Continuous testing: Brands can improve results by testing message timing, offers, channel order, personalization, and discount strategies. Sign up Get a demo Show AI generated summary Abandoned cart flows make you money, more than any other automated flow you set up. That’s what Klaviyo’s product analytics team discovered when they analyzed over 110,000 Klaviyo customers across industries to gather data on abandoned cart open rates, click rates, revenue per recipient (RPR), and more. In this report, we compare abandoned cart flow metrics for the average ecommerce brand to abandoned cart flow metrics for brands performing in the top 10% of Klaviyo users. What you’ll find is that even a basic abandoned cart flow is worth your time and effort, but that optimizing your abandoned cart and overall flow channel mix can pay off even more. For an in-depth analysis of other flows and campaigns across email and text message marketing, download Klaviyo’s 2026 Omnichannel Benchmark Report . Here, let’s dive into a few of the most exciting findings about abandoned cart flows specifically. Abandoned cart flows drive the highest RPR across email and text messaging If you’re looking for a single flow to set up to drive revenue, you’ll find it in the abandoned cart series: abandoned cart flows drive the highest average RPR of all flows, for both email ($6.77) and text messaging ($4.48). Top-performing 10% abandoned cart email flow RPR: $13.70 (3.24% higher than the second-highest RPR flow, the welcome flow) Top-performing 10% abandoned cart text message flow RPR: $8.69 (22.91% higher than the second-highest RPR flow, the welcome flow) Source: Klaviyo’s 2026 Omnichannel Benchmark Report Source: Klaviyo’s 2026 Omnichannel Benchmark Report These rates are attractive even at their average, but some industries have even more exciting abandoned cart results. The home & garden and hardware & home improvement industries, for example, report an average abandoned cart RPR around $15 for email, and the automotive industry reports an average RPR of close to $11 for text message abandoned cart flows. For the top-performing 10% of brands, abandoned cart flow RPR is even more impressive for email: Top-performing 10% of hardware & home improvement: $35.24 Top-performing 10% of home & garden: $28.76 Top-performing 10% of automotive: $27.48 Top-performing 10% of electronics: $24.72 And for text messaging: Top-performing 10% of hardware & home improvement: $28.27 Top-performing 10% of automotive: $18.77 Top-performing 10% of electronics: $17.72 Top-performing 10% of home & garden: $16.57 This is good news across industries, as it shows high abandoned cart flow RPR on both items people need, like furniture, as well as leisure and luxury items, like fancy tech gadgets. Abandoned cart emails come in second to the email welcome series for engagement For email, the average click rate for the abandoned cart flow is 6%, whereas it’s 6.5% for the welcome series. The top-performing 10% of brands see a click rate of 11.3% for the abandoned cart email flow, compared to 13.3% for the welcome series. Source: Klaviyo’s 2026 Omnichannel Benchmark Report For text messaging, the abandoned cart flow yields more engagement than the welcome series, but barely. The average click rate for the abandoned cart text is 10.3%, whereas it’s a close 10% for the welcome series. The top-performing 10% of brands see a click rate of 18.5% for the abandoned cart text flow, compared to 18.3% for the welcome series. Source: Klaviyo’s 2026 Omnichannel Benchmark Report 2026 data indicates it’s just as important to lock in your welcome series as it is your abandoned cart flows, no matter the channel. If one of your goals this year is lowering customer acquisition costs, a great place to start is to treat your omnichannel welcome series strategy with the same level of thought and care as your abandoned cart flows. Browse abandonment emails are just as important for engagement in some industries Despite slightly higher engagement from the welcome series, the abandoned cart email flow still consistently drives high click rates across all industries. This suggests that no matter what industry you’re operating in, an abandoned cart flow is an absolute must. But for some industries, the browse abandonment flow is becoming almost or just as important as the abandoned cart for engagement: The home & garden industry has the highest average abandoned cart email click rate (6.5%), compared to a browse abandonment click rate of 5.8%. For the home & garden industry, the abandoned cart is still more important than their browse abandonment flow. The hardware & home improvement industry also clocks an above-average click rate (6.4%) for their abandoned cart email flow. But what’s interesting here is that browse abandonment flows average a 6.5% click rate, suggesting that flow is at least as important for engagement. For the electronics industry , both email abandonment flows have an average click rate of 6.3%. The automotive industry has a below-average click rate of 5.7% for their abandoned cart email flow, but their browse abandonment flow sees a 6% click rate above the 5.6% average across all verticals. Given what we’re seeing comparatively across email flows for the abandoned cart, browse abandonment, and welcome series, the data suggests it’s important to invest your resources in a diversity of flows. Note that this logic doesn’t necessarily hold for text messages. When compared to browse abandonment, the abandoned cart still comes out on top for click rate across all industries, even though welcome series engagement sees higher engagement in some verticals. Key takeaways to measure and optimize your abandoned cart performance While every brand is different, performance metrics like these will help you gauge whether your abandoned cart flow is knocking it out of the park, doing fine as is, or needs some work to improve. Once you understand what kind of benchmarks your abandoned cart flow could achieve in an ideal world, you’ll be better equipped to track and measure your flow’s performance so that you can start answering questions like: How many messages should be in my abandoned cart flow? The answer depends on your industry, product line, and business goals, but a common sequence might involve 3 messages: a simple email reminder after 2–4 hours, a follow-up text message with a discount after 24 hours, and a final message after 48 hours that includes alternative product recommendations or asks for feedback. What should my abandoned cart flow subject line say? Again, this depends, but a good place to start is personalizing your subject line or text message by including the recipient’s first name and details about the products they left behind in their cart. You can also outsource this thinking to an AI marketing agent that’s trained on the real-time customer data in your CRM. It can make relevant suggestions for personalizing your subject lines or text messages based on real customer behavior and preferences. What channel should my abandoned cart message go out on first?
